newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul takes steps to revive ailing bourse.
newsitem.headline: Seoul takes steps to revive ailing bourse.

text.p: South Korea on Monday unveiled steps to boost share buying by investment firms, but analysts said they saw limited immediate impact on the local market.
The Ministry of Finance and Economy said it would allow three Seoul-based investment firms to raise capital by a combined 260 billion won ($313.8 million).
A ministry statement said the stock market has languished due to a shortage of funds and that the ministry expected part of the capital increases to prompt more share buying.

Analysts, however, doubted the move would have a substantial impact on share prices. "The move reflects that the government was not staying idle and is committed to supporting the stock market. But I see little more than that political statement from the steps," said Yoo Nam-gil, an analyst at Hyundai Securities.

The three investment firms -- Korea Investment Trust Co, Daehan Investment Trust Co and Citizens Investment Trust Management Co -- had been seeking to increase capital to improve their financial structures, it said.
Analysts said major shareholders of the three investment firms were securities and insurance companies, who themselves are significant players on the market.
"It's like moving money from the left hand to the right hand," said Namuh Rhee, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities. "Actual fund influx from outside the market will be limited."
The ministry also said it would soon approve plans by Samsung Securities Co and Ssangyong Investment and Securities Co to set up trust management joint ventures with foreign companies.
It said approvals would be given "in the near future" but gave no timetable.

Samsung Securities, a unit of Samsung Group, plans to form a joint venture with a JP Morgan and Co unit and Ssangyong Investment, a Ssangyong Group unit, with Franklin/Templeton Group, the statement said.
Funds to be raised by the two joint ventures are expected to total between one trillion and 1.5 trillion won once they are established, it said.
It also said the nation's 14 major trust management firms would be encouraged to develop and sell new products that can better accommodate diverse demands for investment instruments.
Analysts said the impact from the government's steps would do little to improve fundamentals that caused the market's current slump.

The composite stock index closed on Monday at this year's lowest level of 716.45, down 14.99 points, or 2.05 percent, from the previous close. This was a fall of 27.4 percent from this year's high of 986.84 set on May 7.

"The current problem with the market is that interest rates are still very high," said Dongbang's Rhee. "So there is no incentive for investment in stocks." Interest for one-year time deposit is about 12 percent.
"There's nothing that the government can do at this moment to help the market," he said.
Analysts said fears of an oversupply of shares also contributed to the stock market's poor tone.
Brokers said the government's plan to sell about 360 billion won worth of shares in state-run Korea Telecom on November 28 and 29 further dampened market sentiment. ($1 = 828.5 won)
